docs.title: Curation Criteria
docs.text: This document defines the quality standards used for selecting resources in Awesome Cryobiology.

docs.title: Repository Philosophy
docs.text:
The goal is not to collect the largest number of links.

The goal is to curate: - scientifically valuable, - educationally useful, - reproducible, - and practically relevant resources.

Quality is prioritized over quantity.

docs.title: Scientific Credibility
docs.text: Resources should: - come from credible journals, institutions, repositories, or communities, - be technically accurate, - and provide meaningful scientific or engineering value.

docs.title: Educational Value
docs.text: Resources that clearly explain: - concepts, - workflows, - engineering systems, - or analysis methods are strongly encouraged.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: Preference is given to resources that include: - metadata, - protocols, - datasets, - code, - or methodological transparency.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text: Preference is given to: - open-access papers, - open-source tools, - reusable educational materials, - and publicly accessible datasets.

docs.title: Technical Utility
docs.text: Useful resources include: - protocols, - software, - workflows, - thermal validation methods, - segmentation pipelines, - and engineering documentation.

docs.title: Licensing and Reuse
docs.text: Resources involving: - figures, - datasets, - code, - or educational material should have clearly reusable licensing where possible.

docs.title: Recommended Resource Types
docs.text:
Strongly encouraged:

  • landmark papers
  • review papers
  • protocols
  • open datasets
  • software tools
  • AI workflows
  • cryomicroscopy guides
  • cryostage engineering resources
  • educational diagrams
  • reproducible pipelines

docs.title: Discouraged Content
docs.text:
The following are discouraged:

  • broken links
  • unverified claims
  • duplicate resources
  • poorly documented repositories
  • inaccessible commercial resources without educational value
  • low-quality AI-generated scientific content without validation

docs.title: Long-Term Goal
docs.text: Awesome Cryobiology aims to become: - a trusted scientific resource, - a reproducibility-focused platform, - and a collaborative ecosystem for cryobiology and cryomicroscopy.

docs.title: Cryobiology Glossary
docs.text: A beginner-friendly glossary of key terms used in cryobiology, cryopreservation, cryomicroscopy, cryoengineering, and low-temperature biology.

docs.title: Antifreeze Proteins
docs.text: Ice-binding proteins found in some organisms that can modify ice crystal growth and inhibit ice recrystallization.

docs.title: Annealing
docs.text: A period during which a frozen sample is held at a specific subzero temperature. Annealing can promote ice crystal growth or recrystallization depending on conditions.

docs.title: Biobanking
docs.text: The organized collection, processing, storage, and management of biological samples for research, clinical, conservation, or therapeutic use.

docs.title: Controlled-Rate Freezing
docs.text: A freezing approach where temperature is reduced according to a defined cooling profile, often to reduce intracellular ice formation and osmotic injury.

docs.title: Cryoinjury
docs.text: Biological damage caused by cooling, freezing, storage at low temperature, or warming. Cryoinjury may involve ice formation, osmotic stress, membrane damage, oxidative stress, and rewarming damage.

docs.title: Cryomicroscopy
docs.text: Microscopy performed during cooling, freezing, storage, or warming to observe ice formation, cell response, phase transitions, or cryoinjury in real time.

docs.title: Cryoprotective Agent
docs.text: A chemical or biomolecule that protects cells, tissues, or biological materials from freezing or vitrification damage. Examples include DMSO, glycerol, ethylene glycol, trehalose, and sucrose.

docs.title: Cryostage
docs.text: A temperature-controlled stage mounted on a microscope to enable imaging under low-temperature conditions.

docs.title: Devitrification
docs.text: The formation of ice crystals from a previously vitrified glassy state, usually during warming. Devitrification can damage biological samples.

docs.title: Directional Freezing
docs.text: A freezing method where a sample experiences a controlled thermal gradient, producing a moving freezing front.

docs.title: DMSO
docs.text: Dimethyl sulfoxide, a widely used permeating cryoprotective agent for mammalian cells and cell therapy products.

docs.title: Glass Transition
docs.text: The temperature range where a liquid-like vitrified material transitions into a glassy solid state without crystallization.

docs.title: Glycerol
docs.text: A permeating cryoprotective agent commonly used in sperm and red blood cell cryopreservation.

docs.title: Ice Nucleation
docs.text: The initial formation of an ice crystal nucleus. Ice nucleation may occur spontaneously or be induced intentionally.

docs.title: Ice Recrystallization
docs.text: The growth of larger ice crystals at the expense of smaller ones during storage or warming. It can contribute to cryoinjury.

docs.title: Intracellular Ice Formation
docs.text: Ice formation inside cells. It is often lethal or highly damaging because it can disrupt membranes, organelles, and intracellular structures.

docs.title: Membrane Integrity
docs.text: The structural and functional state of a cell membrane. It is commonly assessed using dyes such as propidium iodide or SYBR-14/PI combinations.

docs.title: Osmotic Stress
docs.text: Cellular stress caused by water movement across membranes in response to changes in solute concentration.

docs.title: Rewarming Injury
docs.text: Damage that occurs during thawing or warming, including osmotic shock, devitrification, recrystallization, and thermal stress.

docs.title: Solution Effects Injury
docs.text: Cryoinjury caused by increasing solute concentration as extracellular ice forms and excludes solutes into the remaining unfrozen fraction.

docs.title: Splat Cooling Assay
docs.text: A method used to evaluate ice recrystallization inhibition activity by rapidly freezing a small droplet and monitoring ice crystal growth during annealing.

docs.title: Thermal Gradient
docs.text: A spatial temperature difference across a sample or device. Thermal gradients are central to directional freezing and cryostage engineering.

docs.title: Thawing Rate
docs.text: The rate at which a frozen sample is warmed. Thawing rate can strongly influence survival and recrystallization risk.

docs.title: Vitrification
docs.text: A cryopreservation approach where a sample becomes a glass-like solid without ice crystal formation, usually requiring high CPA concentrations and rapid cooling.

docs.title: Ice Recrystallization
docs.text: Resources related to ice recrystallization, IRI-active compounds, microscopy methods, and quantification tools.

docs.title: Reporting Standards for Cryobiology and Cryomicroscopy
docs.text: This document provides recommended metadata and reporting standards for cryobiology, cryopreservation, cryomicroscopy, and thermal imaging experiments.

docs.title: Why Reporting Standards Matter
docs.text:
Cryobiology experiments are highly sensitive to:

  • cooling rate,
  • warming rate,
  • sample geometry,
  • CPA composition,
  • imaging conditions,
  • and thermal history.

Incomplete reporting reduces reproducibility and makes comparison between studies difficult.

docs.title: Biological Information
docs.text:
• Species
  • Cell or tissue type
  • Cell concentration
  • Passage number
  • Donor information where appropriate
  • Viability before freezing

docs.title: Cryoprotective Agents
docs.text:
• CPA type
  • CPA concentration
  • Exposure time
  • Loading procedure
  • Dilution procedure
  • Osmotic equilibration details

docs.title: Cooling Parameters
docs.text:
• Cooling rate
  • Seeding temperature
  • Hold temperatures
  • Thermal gradient
  • Freezing device
  • Cooling medium

docs.title: Storage Parameters
docs.text:
• Storage temperature
  • Storage duration
  • Storage container
  • LN2 vapor or liquid storage

docs.title: Warming Parameters
docs.text:
• Warming rate
  • Warming device
  • Warming medium
  • CPA removal protocol

docs.title: Imaging Metadata
docs.text:
• Microscope type
  • Objective type and magnification
  • Excitation wavelength
  • Emission filters
  • Detector type
  • Laser power
  • Detector gain
  • Exposure time or pixel dwell time
  • Imaging temperature
  • Imaging medium
  • Fluorophores used

docs.title: Thermal Validation
docs.text:
• Sensor type
  • Sensor calibration
  • Spatial thermal measurements
  • Temporal thermal measurements
  • Thermal uncertainty
  • Thermal mapping method

docs.title: Viability and Functional Assays
docs.text:
• Membrane integrity assay
  • ROS assay
  • Mitochondrial assay
  • Motility assay
  • Functional recovery assay
  • Time post-thaw before analysis

docs.title: Recommended Data Practices
docs.text:
• Preserve raw data where possible
  • Use non-destructive file formats
  • Store metadata alongside datasets
  • Include scale bars in microscopy figures
  • Include timestamps for time-lapse data
  • Report software and software versions

docs.title: Suggested Future Standards
docs.text:
• Shared metadata schema for cryomicroscopy
  • Benchmark datasets with standardized annotations
  • Shared thermal validation protocols
  • Reproducible AI evaluation pipelines

docs.title: Cryobiology Troubleshooting Guide
docs.text: A practical troubleshooting guide for cryopreservation, cryomicroscopy, fluorescence imaging, thermal systems, and computational analysis.

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
• Excessive cooling rate
  • Excessive warming delay
  • Intracellular ice formation
  • CPA toxicity
  • Osmotic stress
  • Inadequate equilibration

docs.title: Potential Solutions
docs.text:
• Optimize cooling profile
  • Increase warming rate
  • Adjust CPA exposure time
  • Reduce osmotic shock
  • Validate thermal profiles

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
• Insufficient CPA concentration
  • Slow cooling in vitrification workflows
  • Thermal instability
  • Poor cryostage insulation

docs.title: Potential Solutions
docs.text:
• Increase vitrification efficiency
  • Improve thermal control
  • Validate temperature gradients
  • Improve sample geometry consistency

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
• Slow warming rate
  • Thermal nonuniformity
  • Inadequate warming systems

docs.title: Potential Solutions
docs.text:
• Increase warming rate
  • Reduce sample volume
  • Improve thermal coupling
  • Explore nanowarming strategies

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
• Humidity exposure
  • Inadequate dry-gas purge
  • Poor vacuum isolation

docs.title: Potential Solutions
docs.text:
• Improve dry-gas systems
  • Use vacuum shrouds
  • Reduce environmental humidity
  • Minimize stage exposure time

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
• Incorrect excitation wavelength
  • Low fluorophore concentration
  • Photobleaching
  • Inappropriate filters
  • Thermal effects on fluorophores

docs.title: Potential Solutions
docs.text:
• Validate excitation and emission compatibility
  • Optimize laser power
  • Adjust detector gain
  • Reduce photobleaching exposure
  • Verify fluorophore compatibility under cryogenic conditions

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
• Media autofluorescence
  • Egg-yolk interference
  • Spectral overlap
  • Frost artifacts

docs.title: Potential Solutions
docs.text:
• Optimize imaging medium
  • Adjust filters
  • Reduce background fluorescence
  • Validate fluorophore separation

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
• Thermal expansion
  • Poor mounting
  • Mechanical instability
  • Ice movement

docs.title: Potential Solutions
docs.text:
• Improve stage stability
  • Use immobilization strategies
  • Optimize thermal equilibration
  • Reduce vibration sources

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
• Poor annotations
  • Low signal-to-noise ratio
  • Inconsistent imaging conditions
  • Insufficient training data

docs.title: Potential Solutions
docs.text:
• Improve annotation quality
  • Increase dataset diversity
  • Standardize acquisition settings
  • Use preprocessing pipelines

docs.title: Recommended Long-Term Practices
docs.text:
• Standardize metadata collection
  • Validate thermal systems regularly
  • Preserve raw imaging data
  • Maintain calibration records
  • Use reproducible analysis pipelines
